repetitive

/ri-PET-i-tiv/ — stress on PET · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Repetitive means repeating the same action or pattern again and again, often tediously.

Hour after hour, the work was so repetitive that his mind drifted far from the fluorescent-lit floor while his hands moved on their own.

Worked Example

The assembly line worker performed the same three welding motions hour after hour, and after the first week, she no longer needed to think about what her hands were doing — it had become fully repetitive.

Repetitive is more precise than just saying 'boring' or 'the same action' because it names both the physical fact that the action repeats and the wearying quality that comes from endless repetition — something tedious and mind-numbing by nature.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

redundant: Redundant means duplicated beyond what is needed — a redundant backup, a redundant sentence that restates the last one. Repetitive describes the pattern of the same thing happening again and again, needed or not. A safety system's redundant wiring is welcome; a repetitive chore just keeps coming back.

monotonous: Monotonous means dull from sheer lack of variety — one tone, one view, one flavor — even if nothing is actually repeating as an action. Repetitive requires an action or pattern that recurs again and again. A flat gray wall is monotonous; stamping the same form five hundred times is repetitive.

tedious: Tedious describes how something feels to endure: wearingly boring, whatever the cause — length, difficulty, or dullness. Repetitive describes the structure itself, an action recurring over and over. A repetitive task is often tedious, but a single slow ceremony can be tedious without one repeated element.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

varied: different each time, full of variety

innovative: introducing something new instead of repeating

Where it sits · how relentlessly the same thing returns — unique → varied → recurring → repetitive

unique vs. repetitive: Each snowflake photograph in the gallery was unique, one of a kind with nothing repeated; repetitive sits at the opposite end of the scale, where the same shot is taken again and again until it wears you down.

varied vs. repetitive: A varied paper route with new streets each day keeps the mind engaged; a repetitive one retraces the identical loop until the houses blur together.

recurring vs. repetitive: A recurring choir practice simply happens every Tuesday, but the evening only becomes repetitive when the director drills the same four measures over and over without pause.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: again, back

Root — pet-

Root — pet-: to seek, go toward, rush at (from Latin petere)

Suffix — -itive

Suffix — -itive: tending to, having the quality of (adjective-forming)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (again) + pet- (to seek, go toward) + -itive (tending to) literally means tending to go after something again and again. Compare it with repetition: same prefix, same root, different suffix — -ition builds the noun (the act itself), while -itive builds the adjective (describing whatever keeps doing it). Swap the suffix and the same word parts change jobs.

Use the root in a new word: centripetal

Use the root in a new word: centripetal: The centripetal force of Earth's gravity pulls objects toward the planet's center, keeping satellites in orbit.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Repetitive is the word to use when something repeats the same action or pattern over and over. It usually suggests tedium or weariness but focuses on the pattern itself. When you want to emphasize how boring or tiring it is, try 'tedious' or 'monotonous' instead — they emphasize the feeling rather than the pattern.
